Transphobia is a prejudice — a collection of negative attitudes, feelings, and behaviors — directed at transgender people or at anyone whose gender identity or gender expression does not match the sex they were assigned at birth. These negative attitudes can include fear, contempt, disgust, hostility, or hatred.

The word follows the same pattern as similar words you might already know. Racism is prejudice against people based on their race. Sexism is prejudice based on gender. Homophobia is prejudice against gay or lesbian people. Transphobia fits the same structure — it is prejudice and discrimination targeting transgender and gender-nonconforming people.

To understand transphobia fully, it helps to know who it affects.

Transgender people are those whose gender identity — their deep internal sense of being a man, woman, or something else entirely — is different from the sex they were assigned when they were born. For example, a person who was recorded as male at birth but who is, in fact, a woman.

Nonbinary people are those who don't identify as exclusively or entirely male or female. Their gender falls outside, between, or beyond that binary.

Gender-nonconforming people are those whose outward expression — how they dress, speak, move, or present themselves — doesn't match society's typical expectations for their assigned sex.

Transphobia can be directed at any of these groups. Importantly, a person doesn't need to be "visibly" transgender to experience it — the mere knowledge (or assumption) that someone is transgender can trigger it.
What Transphobia Looks Like in Practice

Transphobia isn't one single thing. It exists on a wide spectrum of severity.

At its most extreme, it manifests as violence — physical assault, threats, intimidation, and even murder. Transgender people, particularly transgender women of color, face disproportionately high rates of violent crime worldwide.

Discrimination is another major form. This includes refusing to hire or promote a transgender person, denying them housing, excluding them from healthcare, or stripping them of legal protections. Refusing a transgender person access to a bathroom that matches their gender identity is a common and much-debated example.

Social and interpersonal transphobia shows up in everyday interactions. Deliberately using the wrong name or wrong pronouns for a transgender person — called "deadnaming" (using the name they no longer use) and "misgendering" (treating them as a gender they are not) — is one of the most common forms. So is ridiculing or mocking transgender people, treating them as confused or mentally ill, denying that their gender identity is real, or revealing that someone is transgender without their permission (called "outing").

At the subtler end of the spectrum are microaggressions — small, often unintentional slights that communicate disrespect or dismissal. Examples include asking intrusive questions about a transgender person's body or medical procedures, making comments like "you look so normal" (which implies that looking normal is surprising), or casually assuming a transgender person must be going through a phase.

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand.

Individual transphobia lives inside a person — in their beliefs, their feelings, and their actions toward transgender people. A landlord who refuses to rent to a transgender tenant, a parent who disowns a transgender child, or a doctor who refuses to provide care to a transgender patient — these are examples of individual transphobia.

Systemic transphobia (also called structural transphobia) is when transphobia is baked into the laws, institutions, policies, and norms of a society. No single hateful person needs to be involved for it to operate — it runs on its own through the way systems are designed. Laws that make it extremely difficult for transgender people to update their legal documents, a medical establishment that historically classified being transgender as a mental illness, official forms and spaces that recognize only a strict male/female binary with no room for anyone else — these are examples of systemic transphobia at work.

The crucial insight here is that a society can harm transgender people through its systems even if most individual people within that society don't consider themselves prejudiced. Systemic transphobia is often harder to see precisely because it doesn't have one face.

Transphobia can be conscious and explicit, where a person is fully aware that they hold negative views toward transgender people and may openly express or act on those views. They might campaign against transgender rights, voice contempt in public, or deliberately mistreat transgender people.

But it can also be unconscious and implicit, where a person doesn't realize they carry transphobic attitudes. They may genuinely believe they treat everyone fairly, yet they might automatically feel uncomfortable around transgender people, make assumptions, or react with subtle hostility without meaning to. This is called "implicit bias," and research shows it is widespread even among people who hold progressive values.

Both forms cause real harm. Unconscious transphobia is not morally neutral just because it is unintentional — impact matters alongside intent.

This concept is especially important and is often overlooked.

Internalized transphobia happens when a transgender person absorbs the negative messages about transgender people that exist in their surrounding culture and begins applying those messages to themselves. They may feel shame about their own identity, doubt themselves, or struggle to accept who they are — not because of any internal flaw, but because the world around them has repeatedly told them that being transgender is wrong, shameful, or unreal.

Internalized transphobia is a product of the environment, not the person. Understanding it is essential for understanding why prejudice causes harm even when it is not directed at someone directly.

Getting this right is important, because the word is sometimes used imprecisely.

Genuine, respectful curiosity is not automatically transphobic. Asking thoughtful questions to learn and understand — when done with care and genuine openness — is generally not transphobia. The line lies in whether questions are intrusive, dehumanizing, or rooted in disbelief rather than curiosity.

Not knowing something is not the same as being transphobic. If you've never been told a person's pronouns, using the wrong ones is a mistake, not an act of hostility. Refusing to correct yourself after being told, however, is a choice.

Policy disagreements are complicated. Not every debate about a policy affecting transgender people is automatically transphobic in itself — though arguments that deny the very validity or existence of transgender identities do fall within the definition of transphobia.

The core question in gray areas is usually: does this attitude or behavior fundamentally reject or diminish a person's gender identity? If so, it is transphobic. If it comes from genuine learning or a good-faith policy disagreement, the answer may be less clear-cut.

Transphobia has serious, documented, and measurable effects on people's lives.

Mental health is profoundly affected. Transgender people experience significantly higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts. Research has consistently found that these outcomes are strongly linked to experiences of rejection, discrimination, and violence — not to being transgender itself. When transgender people are accepted and supported, these rates drop dramatically.

Physical safety is a serious concern. Transgender people — particularly transgender women of color — face elevated rates of violence, hate crimes, and murder in many parts of the world.

Economic harm is well-documented. Discrimination in hiring, housing, and education leads to disproportionately high rates of poverty and homelessness among transgender people.

Healthcare is disrupted. Fear of discrimination causes many transgender people to avoid seeking medical care, leading to worse health outcomes across the board.

Social exclusion compounds everything else. Family rejection, loss of friendships, being pushed out of religious communities, and social ostracism are common experiences that isolate transgender people at the times when they need support most.

These are not small or abstract consequences. They represent real reductions in the quality and length of transgender people's lives.
A Few Related Terms Worth Knowing

Cissexism is a broader term for the assumption — often built into social structures — that cisgender (non-transgender) identities are more natural, legitimate, or normal than transgender ones. Think of it as the cultural water in which individual transphobia swims.

Transmisogyny is a specific form of transphobia targeted at transgender women. It combines transphobia with misogyny (prejudice against women), recognizing that transgender women often face a compounded form of discrimination. The term was coined by author and biologist Julia Serano.

Deadnaming refers specifically to calling a transgender person by the name they used before their transition — a name they have left behind. It is considered a form of transphobia when done deliberately.

Misgendering means referring to a transgender person using a gender or pronouns that don't match who they are. When done deliberately and repeatedly, it is considered a form of transphobia.

Transphobia is a prejudice — rooted in fear, contempt, hostility, or hatred — directed at transgender and gender-nonconforming people. Like racism and sexism, it operates at both the individual level (in how people think and act) and the systemic level (in how laws and institutions are built). It ranges from violent hate crimes to subtle everyday dismissals. It can be conscious or unconscious. It can even be internalized by transgender people themselves. And it causes serious, measurable harm to the mental health, physical safety, economic wellbeing, and social lives of the people it targets.

Understanding transphobia — where it comes from, what it looks like, and what it does — is the foundation for recognizing it, confronting it, and reducing the harm it causes.
